Short answer
- Archiving: you move a record out of active systems into long‑term storage where it’s preserved and still subject to the retention schedule and controls. It’s retained, searchable (maybe limited), and recoverable.
- Deleting: you remove the record (soft delete or permanent/hard delete) so it is no longer available — a disposition action that should only happen when the retention schedule and any holds allow it.

Key practical differences

- Purpose
  - Archive: preserve records for future reference, compliance, audit, or historical purposes while freeing active systems.
  - Delete: dispose of records that have met their retention requirements (or are otherwise approved for destruction).

- Legal & compliance implications
  - Archive: continues to meet legal/regulatory obligations; supports e‑discovery and audits.
  - Delete: must be justified by the retention schedule and cleared of legal holds; improper deletion risks spoliation, regulatory fines, or audit findings.

- Recoverability & accessibility
  - Archive: generally recoverable (may have restricted access or slower retrieval).
  - Delete: may be recoverable only for a short time (soft delete) or not at all (secure/hard delete). Backups may retain copies unless specifically purged.

- Metadata, chain of custody & audit trail
  - Archive: metadata and audit logs should be preserved to show provenance and retention status.
  - Delete: require documentation of disposition (who, when, why) and proof that deletion was completed according to policy.

- Technical differences
  - Archive: often moves to lower‑cost storage with different access controls, indexing, or format conversions.
  - Delete: can be a logical delete (flagged, hidden) or physical purge (overwritten, secure wipe). Backups and replicas complicate true removal.

- Interaction with holds
  - Archive: records under legal/regulatory hold remain protected; archiving does not circumvent holds.
  - Delete: must not occur if a legal/regulatory hold is in place — holds typically override the retention schedule.

Practical rules of thumb / recommended checklist before deleting
1. Confirm retention period has fully expired per the retention schedule.
2. Verify no active legal/regulatory holds, investigations, or litigation holds apply.
3. Obtain required approvals (records manager, legal, compliance) if policy requires.
4. Check backups/replicas and ensure disposition covers them or documents why not.
5. Select appropriate deletion method (soft vs hard; secure wiping for sensitive data).
6. Record the disposition (what was deleted, why, who approved, when) in an audit log.
7. Retain proof of deletion where required by policy or regulation.

When to archive vs delete (examples)
- Archive: employee personnel files after active employment ends but are still within retention; historical project records needed for audits.
- Delete: draft marketing emails that reached end of retention and are not subject to hold; transient logs that are explicitly scheduled for disposal.

Operational suggestions
- Automate retention enforcement where possible but ensure automated jobs respect holds.
- Keep clear mappings from record types to retention actions (archive vs destroy).
- Train staff so operational teams don’t accidentally delete records that should be archived.
- Periodically audit retention/disposition processes and logs to demonstrate compliance.

If you want, I can draft a short “pre‑disposition checklist” or example policy language you can drop into your retention schedule or procedures.
